claim: Cutaneous malignant melanoma is associated with high levels of intermittent sun exposure rather than chronic exposure.
source: Cutaneous malignant melanoma (MM) is well known to be associated with high levels of sun exposure. However, this is only true for intermittent rather than chronic exposures, with indoor workers having a higher risk for MM than outdoor workers (Gandini et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gandini et al., 2005

claim: Indoor workers have a higher risk for malignant melanoma than outdoor workers.
source: However, this is only true for intermittent rather than chronic exposures, with indoor workers having a higher risk for MM than outdoor workers (Gandini et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gandini et al., 2005

claim: Lentigo maligna melanoma is invariably linked to chronic sun exposure.
source: One melanoma subtype, lentigo maligna melanoma (LMM), is invariably linked to chronic sun exposure.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Genetic variation controls skin color, DNA repair capability, propensity to burn, failure of programmed death of damaged cells, and other factors that control melanocyte behavior, contributing to individual melanoma risk.
source: Individual risk for the development of MM is in part due to the number of UVR-induced mutations incurred (i.e. the environmental factor), but it is also due to genetic variation that controls skin color (degree of protection due to pigment), DNA repair capability (DiGiovanna and Kraemer, 2012), propensity to burn (inflammation), failure of programmed death of a damaged cell, and/or other factors that control melanocyte behavior (Sample and He, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to DiGiovanna and Kraemer, 2012 and Sample and He, 2018

claim: GWAS point to genes regulating cell division control, DNA repair, and pigmentation as main players in conferring melanoma risk.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) point to genes regulating aspects of cell division control (e.g. CDKN2A/MTAP, PLA2G6, TERT), DNA repair (e.g. PARP1, APEX1, ATM), and pigmentation (e.g. MC1R, ASIP, TYR, SLC45A2, TYR) as the main players in conferring MM risk (Gerstenblith et al., 2010; Duffy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerstenblith et al., 2010 and Duffy et al., 2018

claim: Only a small fraction of the variance in melanoma risk is explained by known genes, suggesting other genes are involved in conferring melanoma risk in the general population.
source: However only a small fraction of the variance in MM risk is explained by these genes, suggesting that there are still other genes involved in conferring MM risk in the general population (Hulur et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hulur et al., 2017

claim: Superficial spreading melanomas are sometimes found on sun-exposed body sites, but more often on non-sun exposed sites.
source: The most common superficial spreading melanomas (SSM) are sometimes found on sun-exposed body sites, but more often on non-sun exposed sites, and there can be great diversity in terms of the number of UVR signature mutations in individual lesions (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukhopadhyay et al., 2017

claim: There is great diversity in the number of UVR signature mutations in individual melanoma lesions.
source: The most common superficial spreading melanomas (SSM) are sometimes found on sun-exposed body sites, but more often on non-sun exposed sites, and there can be great diversity in terms of the number of UVR signature mutations in individual lesions (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukhopadhyay et al., 2017

claim: Less intense UVR exposures may be more important for skin cancer induction than more intense doses which cause more apoptosis.
source: There is in vivo evidence that less intense exposures may be more important for skin cancer induction than more intense doses which cause more apoptosis (Lan et al., 2016), and even for a single exposure there are significant differences in skin responses between the same dose (i.e. the same levels of DNA damage) administered with high intensity over a short period versus a low intensity for a longer period (Iida et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lan et al., 2016 and Iida et al., 2016

claim: There are significant differences in skin responses between the same UVR dose administered with high intensity over a short period versus low intensity for a longer period.
source: There is in vivo evidence that less intense exposures may be more important for skin cancer induction than more intense doses which cause more apoptosis (Lan et al., 2016), and even for a single exposure there are significant differences in skin responses between the same dose (i.e. the same levels of DNA damage) administered with high intensity over a short period versus a low intensity for a longer period (Iida et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iida et al., 2016

claim: Skin can protect itself via pigmentation responses (tanning) and by 'photo-adaption', which is independent of pigmentation levels.
source: Our skin can protect itself via pigmentation responses (tanning), but also by 'photo-adaption', which is independent of pigmentation levels (Palmer et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palmer et al., 2006

claim: Natural genetic variation can confer resistance to many cancer types in mice.
source: Natural genetic variation can confer resistance to many cancer types in mice (Balmain, 2002), and it is of great interest to determine why this is so.
evidence: Supported by citation to Balmain, 2002

claim: Most mouse melanoma models rapidly develop tumours after neonatal UVR exposure.
source: Most mouse MM models rapidly develop tumours after neonatal UVR exposure.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Mouse melanoma models have provided tractable experimental systems to determine a melanoma action spectrum, assess which type of UVR-induced DNA adducts are required, and study the role of UVR-induced DNA damage, inflammation, and immunosuppression.
source: Such models have provided tractable experimental systems to determine a MM action spectrum (De Fabo et al., 2004), to assess which type of UVR-induced DNA adducts are required, and to study the role of UVR-induced DNA damage, inflammation, and immunosuppression (Walker, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Fabo et al., 2004 and Walker, 2008

claim: A single neonatal UVR exposure does not accelerate melanoma onset via the acquisition of unrepaired UVR-induced damage leading to mutations in important cancer genes.
source: We have shown previously that it is not via the acquisition of unrepaired UVR-induced damage leading to mutations in important cancer genes (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukhopadhyay et al., 2016

claim: There is a muted inflammatory response to UVR in neonates associated with immunosuppression.
source: A number of factors have been proposed to play a role: 1) there is a muted inflammatory response to UVR in neonates associated with immunosuppression (Wolnicka-Glubisz et al., 2007); 15,16), Muller et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wolnicka-Glubisz et al., 2007 and Muller et al., 2008

claim: There is a heightened sensitivity of neonatal melanocytes to proliferate following UVR that is driven by inflammatory cytokines, especially interferon-γ.
source: there is a heightened sensitivity of neonatal melanocytes to proliferate following UVR (Walker et al., 209) that is driven by inflammatory cytokines, especially interferon-γ (Zaidi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Walker et al., 2009 and Zaidi et al., 2011

claim: Somatic NRAS mutation is carried by 27% of melanomas.
source: Somatic NRAS mutation is carried by 27% of MMs (http://www.cbioportal.org), and in ~90% of MMs the p16/CDK4/pRb pathway is deregulated via mutations in CDKN2A, CDK4, or RB1, and/or CDK4 or CCND1 amplification (Sheppard and McArthur, 2013).
evidence: Supported by reference to cbioportal.org database

claim: In approximately 90% of melanomas the p16/CDK4/pRb pathway is deregulated via mutations in CDKN2A, CDK4, or RB1, and/or CDK4 or CCND1 amplification.
source: Somatic NRAS mutation is carried by 27% of MMs (http://www.cbioportal.org), and in ~90% of MMs the p16/CDK4/pRb pathway is deregulated via mutations in CDKN2A, CDK4, or RB1, and/or CDK4 or CCND1 amplification (Sheppard and McArthur, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheppard and McArthur, 2013

claim: The Collaborative Cross is a set of recombinant inbred mouse strains generated from eight original founder strains, designed to enable rapid gene mapping.
source: To do so, we utilized the Collaborative Cross (CC), a set of recombinant inbred mouse strains generated from eight original founder strains, designed to enable rapid gene mapping (Churchill et al., 2004; Morahan et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Churchill et al., 2004 and Morahan et al., 2008

claim: The Collaborative Cross is ideal for systematic analysis studies to discover modifier genes for complex diseases.
source: The CC is ideal for systematic analysis studies to discover modifier genes for complex diseases.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about the CC resource

claim: Mice from each inbred CC strain may be considered as 'clones' of each other.
source: Mice from each inbred CC strain may be considered as 'clones' of each other.
evidence: Stated as a property of the CC resource

claim: The diversity outbred (DO) population consists of mice descended from the same eight founders as the CC, generated as outbred stock.
source: Related to the CC is the diversity outbred (DO) population, in which mice descended from the same eight founders are generated as outbred stock (Churchill et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Churchill et al., 2012

claim: The DO system allows very high levels of heterozygosity and recombination of CC founder alleles, but each DO mouse is genetically unique and not reproducible for experimentation requiring testing of multiple mice.
source: The DO system allows very high levels of heterozygosity and recombination of CC founder alleles, but each DO mouse is genetically unique and not reproducible for experimentation requiring testing of multiple mice.
evidence: Stated as a property of the DO resource

claim: BRAFV600E mutation is more common than NRASQ61K in melanoma overall.
source: Given that BRAFV600E mutation is more common than NRASQ61K in MM overall, we studied the inducible BrafV600E model developed by the MacMahon lab (Dankort et al., 2009) combined with the knock-in mutant Cdk4R24C mouse.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: There was no significant difference in melanoma age of onset between Cdk4R24C/R24C::Tyr-CreER::BrafV600E mice with Braf induced before UVR, after UVR, or without UVR.
source: Surprisingly, we saw no significant difference in MM age of onset between any cohort (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Melanoma is not observed in Cdk4R24C/R24C mice without carrying a melanocyte-specific Ras pathway mutation, with or without neonatal UVR.
source: Melanoma is not observed in Cdk4R24C/R24C mice without carrying a melanocyte-specific Ras pathway mutation, with or without neonatal UVR (Hacker et al., 2006), showing that in our experiments with the Cdk4R24C/R24C::Tyr-CreER::BrafV600E model, BrafV600E must have been induced by the tamox application.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hacker et al., 2006

claim: Using the Cdk4R24C/R24C::Tyr-NRASQ61K model, a single neonatal UVR exposure significantly accelerated melanoma age of onset.
source: In contrast, using the Cdk4R24C/R24C::Tyr-NRASQ61K model (Ferguson et al., 2010) the single neonatal UVR exposure significantly accelerated MM age of onset (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 1D, with citation to Ferguson et al., 2010

claim: In the Trp53F/F::Tyr-Cre(ER)::Tyr-NRAS model, tamoxifen treatment (Trp53 deletion in melanocytes) accelerated both spontaneous and UVR-induced melanoma.
source: Tamox treatment (i.e. Trp53 deletion in melanocytes) accelerated both spontaneous and UVR-induced MM.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: In the Trp53F/F::Tyr-Cre(ER)::Tyr-NRAS model, there was no difference in melanoma onset whether or not Trp53 was deleted before or after neonatal UVR.
source: But there was no difference in MM onset whether or not Trp53 was deleted before or after neonatal UVR.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: For both BrafV600E and Trp53-inducible models, the ability of neonatal UVR to accelerate melanoma may not be dependent upon whether the engineered mutation is present in melanocytes at the time of UVR exposure.
source: Thus for both BrafV600E and Trp53-inducible models the ability of neonatal UVR to accelerate MM may not be dependent upon whether the engineered mutation is present in melanocytes at the time of UVR exposure.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data

claim: An oncogenic mutation in melanocytes seems to be a prerequisite for UVR to accelerate melanoma.
source: But an oncogenic mutation in melanocytes seems to be a prerequisite.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data

claim: The Cdk4::NRAS model was best suited for breeding with CC mice to look for QTLs associated with UVR-dependent melanoma.
source: In sum, the Cdk4::NRAS model was best suited for breeding with CC mice to look for QTLs associated with UVR-dependent MM.
evidence: Based on inference from comparative experimental data

claim: A major effect QTL for spontaneous melanoma age of onset was identified on mouse chromosome 16 at the -Log10(P) −1 interval = 14.8–21.4 megabases, a region containing 45 genes.
source: We identified a major effect QTL on mouse chromosome (chr) 16. The -Log10(P) −1 interval = 14.8–21.4 megabases (Mb), a region containing 45 genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on QTL mapping data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The causal variant for early age of onset of spontaneous melanoma was derived from the 129/SvJ founder.
source: Examination of the founder haplotype coefficients in the significantly linked interval on chromosome 16 showed that the causal variant for early age of onset of MM was derived from the 129/SvJ founder (hereafter termed 129S).
evidence: Based on analysis of founder haplotype coefficients from QTL mapping data

claim: Eight candidate genes within the chromosome 16 QTL interval were identified based on 129S-specific variants: Prkdc, Pkp2, Yars2, Arvcf, Gp1bb, and Abcc5.
source: Mining the Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases for 129S-specific variants revealed eight candidates, two of which (Prkdc and Arvcf) carry non-synonymous mutations (Figure 2D), while all 8 (Prkdc, Pkp2, Yars2, Arvcf, Gp1bb, and Abcc5) had 129S-specific single nucleotide potentially regulatory polymorphisms (SNPs) in their 5' or 3' UTR, or introns.
evidence: Based on mining Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases, shown in Figure 2D

claim: Prkdc and Arvcf carry non-synonymous mutations on the 129S allele.
source: Mining the Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases for 129S-specific variants revealed eight candidates, two of which (Prkdc and Arvcf) carry non-synonymous mutations (Figure 2D)
evidence: Based on mining Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases, shown in Figure 2D

claim: The six candidate genes (Prkdc, Pkp2, Yars2, Arvcf, Gp1bb, Abcc5) are expressed in neonatal mouse skin and/or hair follicle, including in melanocytes.
source: Next, we looked at skin gene expression of the six candidates. They are expressed in neonatal mouse skin and/or hair follicle, including in melanocytes, as published in the Hair Gel database (Sennett et al., 2015) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on data from the Hair Gel database (Sennett et al., 2015), shown in Figure 2E

claim: Lamp3 was the only gene within the chromosome 16 QTL region significantly differentially expressed between susceptible (129S allele-carrying) and resistant strains (non 129S allele-carrying).
source: Only one gene (Lamp3, lysosomal-associated membrane protein 3) of the potential expressed sequences within the region was significantly differentially expressed between the susceptible and resistant strains assessed (Figure 2F)
evidence: Based on RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Prkdc carries two missense mutations on the 129S allele, one defined as deleterious by SIFT.
source: Prkdc carried two missense mutations, one defined as deleterious by SIFT.
evidence: Based on SIFT analysis of sequence variants

claim: The Prkdc R2140C mutation was previously mapped and validated as a modifier of lymphomagenesis, breast cancer, and adenoma associated with ionizing radiation.
source: This is the same Prkdc (R2140C) mutation previously mapped and validated as a modifier of lymphomagenesis (Mori et al., 2001), breast cancer (Yu et al., 2001), and adenoma associated with ionizing radiation (Degg et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mori et al., 2001, Yu et al., 2001, and Degg et al., 2003

claim: PRKDC plays a critical role in ensuring genome integrity and in cancer by mediating ligation of double stranded breaks in DNA.
source: PRKDC (also known as DNA-PKc) plays a critical role in ensuring genome integrity and in cancer in general by mediating ligation of double stranded breaks in DNA (Goodwin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goodwin et al., 2015

claim: Arvcf is a catenin protein family member that plays an important role in the formation of adherens complexes.
source: The other gene within the interval that is a likely candidate is Arvcf (armadillo repeat gene deleted in velo-cardio-facial syndrome), a catenin protein family member. This family plays an important role in the formation of adherens complexes, which are thought to facilitate communication between the inside and outside environments of a cell.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Arvcf function

claim: Arvcf carries a missense mutation on the causal 129S allele that is defined as tolerated by SIFT.
source: This carries on the causal 129S allele a missense mutation that is defined as tolerated by SIFT, so is perhaps not as likely to be the causal gene.
evidence: Based on SIFT analysis of sequence variants

claim: Prkdc is the most likely candidate gene for the spontaneous melanoma QTL on chromosome 16, with Acvrf and Lamp3 as less likely candidates.
source: In sum, while we cannot in effect rule out another gene within the region, the most likely candidate is Prkdc, since it carries a missense mutation on the causal allele shown before to confer cancer susceptibility, with Acvrf and Lamp3 arguably less likely candidates.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including sequence variants, SIFT predictions, and prior literature

claim: Other genes involved in sensing DNA damage and repairing double stranded breaks (e.g. PARP1, ATM, APEX1) are in linkage disequilibrium with SNPs associated with melanoma risk in GWAS.
source: We noted that other genes involved in sensing DNA damage and repairing double stranded breaks (e.g. PARP1, ATM, APEX1) are in linkage disequilibrium with SNPs associated with melanoma risk in GWAS (Hulur et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hulur et al., 2017

claim: PARP1 and APEX1 are in the top 300 most significantly correlated genes with PRKDC expression in non-sun exposed human skin across the GTEx cohort.
source: PARP1 (at 170, r = 0.46, p=2×10−16), and APEX1 (at 287, r = 0.43, p=8×10−14) were in the top 300 most significantly correlated genes with PRKDC.
evidence: Based on analysis of GTEx gene expression data

claim: ATR was in the top 105 most significantly correlated genes with PRKDC expression in non-sun exposed human skin across the GTEx cohort.
source: ATM was not in the top 500, but its relative ATR was at number 105 (r = 0.49, p=4×10−16).
evidence: Based on analysis of GTEx gene expression data

claim: A major effect QTL for UVR-induced melanoma age of onset was identified on mouse chromosome 1 at the -Log10(P) −1 interval = 187.8–189.2 Mb, a region containing 10 genes.
source: We identified a major effect QTL on mouse chr.1 (-Log10(P) −1 interval = 187.8–189.2 Mb) (Figure 3C), a region containing 10 genes.
evidence: Based on QTL mapping data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The causal allele for UVR-induced melanoma was carried by AJ and NOD founder strains.
source: The causal allele was carried by AJ and NOD.
evidence: Based on analysis of founder haplotype coefficients from QTL mapping data

claim: Four candidate genes carrying variants specific to the AJ/NOD causal allele were identified: Tgfb2, Rrp15, Spata17, and Gpatch2.
source: Mining the Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases for NOD/AJ-specific variants revealed four candidates carrying variants specific to the causal allele (Tgfb2, Rrp15, Spata17, and Gpatch2).
evidence: Based on mining Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases

claim: Rrp15 was the only candidate gene in the chromosome 1 QTL interval carrying missense mutations.
source: Rrp15 was the only one carrying missense mutations (Figure 3D)
evidence: Based on mining Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases, shown in Figure 3D

claim: Tgfb2, Spata17, and Gpatch2 had AJ/NOD-specific single nucleotide polymorphisms in their 5' or 3' UTR, or introns.
source: while the other three genes (Tgfb2, Spata17, and Gpatch2), had AJ/NOD-specific single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in their 5' or 3' UTR, or introns (Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on mining Sanger Mouse Genomes and ENCODE databases, shown in Figure 3E

claim: All candidate genes except Spata17 were expressed in skin according to the Hair Gel database.
source: Next we looked at the Hair Gel database to determine whether these genes were expressed in skin. All but Spata17 were, essentially ruling this gene out as a candidate (Figure 3F).
evidence: Based on data from the Hair Gel database, shown in Figure 3F

claim: There were no significantly differentially expressed genes in skin between AJ, NOD, and FVB (which carry the Chr. 1 allele) and B6, DBA, and 129S (which do not).
source: We then looked at skin gene expression (Supplementary file 1) between AJ, NOD, and FVB, which carry the Chr. one allele, and B6, DBA, and 129S which do not (Figure 3G). There were no significantly differentially expressed genes between groups, suggesting a missense rather than a regulatory causal variant.
evidence: Based on RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Rrp15 is the best candidate gene for the UVR-induced melanoma QTL on chromosome 1.
source: Thus, while we cannot rule out Tgfb2 and Gpatch2, by those criteria Rrp15 is the best candidate.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including expression data and sequence variants

claim: The causal AJ/NOD allele carried two Rrp15 missense variants, both defined by SIFT as likely to be 'tolerated'.
source: The causal allele (AJ/NOD) carried two Rrp15 missense variants, both defined by SIFT as likely to be 'tolerated'.
evidence: Based on SIFT analysis of sequence variants

claim: The Rrp15 variant at amino acid 117 (Glu > Gln) is most likely to be the causal mutation.
source: But one at amino acid 117 is most likely to be the causal mutation given that it is a Glu > Gln change, whereas the other is Ala > Val, which is likely to be silent.
evidence: Based on inference from the nature of the amino acid changes

claim: Rrp15 encodes a ribosomal subunit that is part of pre 40S and pre 60S subunits that is important for rRNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis.
source: Rrp15 encodes a ribosomal subunit that is part of pre 40S and pre 60S subunits that is important for rRNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about Rrp15 function

claim: Rrp15 knockout in vitro causes nucleolar stress by activating the Mdm2-Trp53 axis, and subsequently a G1-S phase cell cycle blockage.
source: Furthermore, Rrp15 knockout in vitro causes nucleolar stress by activating the Mdm2-Trp53 axis, and subsequently a G1-S phase cell cycle blockage (De Marchis et al., 2005; Dong et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Marchis et al., 2005 and Dong et al., 2017

claim: Deregulation of the ribosome complex decreases the fidelity and patterns of mRNA translation and many other downstream events.
source: Deregulation of the ribosome complex decreases the fidelity and patterns of mRNA translation and many other downstream events (Quin et al., 2014; Pelletier et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Quin et al., 2014 and Pelletier et al., 2018

claim: Ribosome deregulation can affect cell behaviour via p53-independent mechanisms.
source: Although much of the effect on cell behaviour is via altering the stabilisation of p53 by Mdm2, this can also occur via p53-independent mechanisms (James et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to James et al., 2014

claim: The predicted causal SNPs in Rrp15 do not segregate with fast melanoma onset in DO mice.
source: As seen in Figure 3H, the predicted causal SNPs in Rrp15 do not segregate with fast MM onset as they did in the CC strains.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Lack of penetrance of the Rrp15 allele in DO mice was hypothesized to be due to the introduction of additional resistance alleles elsewhere in the genome.
source: We hypothesized that lack of penetrance of the Rrp15 allele was due to the introduction of additional resistance alleles elsewhere in the genome due to the high levels of recombinations and heterozygosity in the DO genomes.
evidence: Based on speculation about genetic mechanisms

claim: After two backcrosses of transgenic-DO mice onto C57BL/6, the penetrance of the causal Rrp15 variant was restored: mice carrying the NOD/AJ alleles of Rrp15 had significantly earlier melanoma onset.
source: We found that the penetrance of the causal Rrp15 variant was restored on backcrossing: mice carrying the NOD/AJ alleles of Rrp15 had significantly earlier MM onset (Figure 3J).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3J

claim: The propensity for neonatal UVR to accelerate melanoma is highly dependent upon genetic background influences.
source: Thus, the propensity for neonatal UVR to accelerate melanoma is highly dependent upon genetic background influences.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data

claim: There are additional potential resistance alleles which can, if present, interact with the Rrp15 susceptibility allele.
source: In addition, there are additional potential resistance alleles which can, if present, interact with the Rrp15 susceptibility allele.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data

claim: In resistant CC strains, neonatal UVR does not accelerate melanoma onset at all or does so by a very small amount, whereas for susceptible strains melanoma onset was accelerated by more than 300 days.
source: In resistant CC strains, neonatal UVR does not accelerate MM onset at all (e.g. HOE, BAX2), or does so by a very small amount, whereas for susceptible strains MM onset was accelerated by more than 300 days (e.g. SEH, XAJ2) as seen in Figure 3K and L.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figures 3K and 3L

claim: The effectiveness of UVR in accelerating melanoma is independent of pigmentation status (albino vs pigmented).
source: The phenotype is independent of pigmentation status (albino vs pigmented) (Figure 3L).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 3L

claim: There was a peak of suggestive significance for UVR effectiveness at chromosome 1, overlapping with the QTL detected for UVR-induced age of onset, containing the Rrp15 gene.
source: While this does not provide enough power to detect genome-wide significant linkage to this phenotype, there was a peak of suggestive significance at chromosome 1 p, overlapping with the QTL detected for UVR-induced age of onset, containing the Rrp15 gene, with the NOD allele showing a different coefficient from the other strains.
evidence: Based on QTL mapping data

claim: At 6 hr after neonatal UVR exposure, there is strong significant evidence of ribosome biogenesis occurring, with downregulation of various metabolic pathways compared to control untreated skin.
source: At 6 hr after UVR exposure, one can see strong significant evidence of ribosome biogenesis occurring, with downregulation of various metabolic pathways compared to control untreated skin (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on gene expression data from Illumina Beadchips

claim: At 10 hr post-UVR, metabolic activity is still suppressed, but DNA replication is either already occurring or about to occur for repair and reconstruction of damaged cells, and upregulated p53 signaling was observed.
source: At 10 hr, post-UVR metabolic activity is still suppressed, but DNA replication is either already occurring to some extent, or about to occur for repair and reconstruction of damaged cells. Upregulated p53 signaling was also observed.
evidence: Based on gene expression data from Illumina Beadchips

claim: At 24 hr post UVR, various pathways involved in cell proliferation (ribosomes and translation, metabolism) and reconstruction (extracellular matrix, metabolism) are significantly activated in the epidermis.
source: At 24 hr post UVR various pathways involved in cell proliferation (ribosomes and translation, metabolism) and reconstruction (extracellular matrix, metabolism) are significantly activated in the epidermis.
evidence: Based on gene expression data from Illumina Beadchips

claim: At 3 days after UVR, there was a striking loss of immune markers in the epidermis, mostly reflecting UVR-induced migration of epidermal Langerhans cells to the dermis.
source: There was a striking loss of immune markers in the epidermis, mostly reflecting UVR-induced migration of epidermal Langerhans cells to the dermis as expected.
evidence: Based on gene expression data from separate epidermis and dermis samples

claim: At 3 days after UVR, a strong gene expression cluster for genes involved in melanogenesis was observed in the epidermis, reflecting the presence of melanocytes in the UVR-exposed epidermis.
source: We also saw a strong gene expression cluster for genes involved in melanogenesis, reflecting the presence of melanocytes in the UVR-exposed epidermis, but not in control skin at the time-point 3 d after UVR.
evidence: Based on gene expression data from separate epidermis samples

claim: At 3 days after UVR, in the dermis, networks reflecting increased cellular activity were observed, in particular upregulation of kinases and interferon-induced enzymes.
source: In the dermis, we observed networks reflecting increased cellular activity, in particular upregulation of kinases and interferon-induced enzymes.
evidence: Based on gene expression data from separate dermis samples

claim: At 3 days after UVR, in the dermis, a signal for myeloid cells was observed, presumably reflecting the influx of macrophages.
source: But in contrast to the epidermis, in the dermis we also observed a signal for myeloid cells, presumably reflecting the influx of macrophages, which occurs maximally at around this time post UVR (Handoko et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on gene expression data from separate dermis samples and citation to Handoko et al., 2013

claim: Rrp15 was the only candidate gene within the chr.1 QTL region significantly changed in expression after neonatal UVR.
source: Rrp15 was the only one of the chr.1 candidates significantly changed in expression by UVR (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on gene expression data shown in Figure 5B

claim: In a study of UVR-treated cultured melanocytes, ribosome metabolism was the most significantly altered pathway at 6, 12, and 24 hr after UVR.
source: But we note that in a study of UVR-treated cultured melanocytes, ribosome metabolism was the most significantly altered pathway at 6, 12, and 24 hr after UVR (López et al., 2015), as in our whole skin studies.
evidence: Supported by citation to López et al., 2015

claim: Changes in RRP15 gene expression are correlated with ribosome biogenesis, DNA damage recognition and repair, transcription, and splicing in human skin.
source: As expected changes in RRP15 gene expression are correlated with ribosome biogenesis, but also many other aspects of cell behavior, including DNA damage recognition and repair, transcription, and splicing.
evidence: Based on analysis of GTEx gene expression data

claim: Across six laboratory strains, there were no differences in the capacity to remove CPDs, as measured by the proportion of skin cells carrying them post-UVR.
source: First, across the six laboratory strains we found no differences in the capacity to remove CPDs, as measured by the proportion of skin cells carrying them post-UVR.
evidence: Based on immunohistochemical staining data

claim: There was great variation between various laboratory strains in the size and timing of the melanocyte and myeloid cell responses after UVR.
source: However, there was great variation between the various strains in the size and timing of the melanocyte and myeloid cell responses after UVR (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 6A

claim: None of the commonly purported mechanisms by which UVR exacerbates melanoma (CPD removal, melanocyte proliferation, neutrophil influx, macrophage influx) were significantly associated with onset of UVR-induced melanoma when strains were stratified by Rrp15 allele status.
source: When compared in this way none of these commonly purported mechanisms by which UVR exacerbates MM were significantly associated with onset of UVR-induced MM, although we found a non-significant trend for the susceptible strains to show higher levels of neutrophil influx at d1 after UVR.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of immunohistochemical data

claim: There was a non-significant trend for susceptible strains to show higher levels of neutrophil influx at day 1 after UVR.
source: When compared in this way none of these commonly purported mechanisms by which UVR exacerbates MM were significantly associated with onset of UVR-induced MM, although we found a non-significant trend for the susceptible strains to show higher levels of neutrophil influx at d1 after UVR.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of immunohistochemical data

claim: No correlation was found between melanoma age of onset and the measured phenotypes (CPD removal, melanocyte proliferation, neutrophil influx, macrophage influx), although day 1 neutrophil infiltration was nearest to significance.
source: As an additional assessment, we performed a correlation test between MM age of onset and the phenotypes measured and found no significant correlation, although d1 neutrophil infiltration was nearest to significance.
evidence: Based on statistical correlation analysis

claim: Anti-Ly6g treatment significantly depleted neutrophil influx after neonatal UVR.
source: Anti-Ly6g treatment significantly depleted neutrophil influx after neonatal UVR (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Inhibition of neutrophil influx did not suppress UVR-induced melanoma genesis.
source: We exposed two cohorts of Cdk4::NRAS mice to anti-Ly6g anti-neutrophil depleting Ab, or PBS control respectively, then performed a longitudinal study for MM age of onset, but saw no difference in the age of onset of MM between cohorts (Figure 6E). Thus, inhibition of the neutrophil influx did not suppress UVR-induced genesis.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: Different genes mediate spontaneous versus UVR-induced melanoma susceptibility.
source: One of the most striking findings from our study was that the genetic polymorphisms modifying MM onset were very different between spontaneous and UV-induced disease (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on comparison of QTL mapping results for spontaneous vs UVR-induced melanoma

claim: BrafV600E induced in melanocytes in utero is incompatible with embryonic viability.
source: For example, BrafV600E induced in melanocytes in utero is incompatible with embryonic viability (e.g. Dankort et al., 2009), whereas in a non-inducible transgenic BrafV600E models it is not (Wurm et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dankort et al., 2009 and Wurm et al., 2012

claim: In a non-inducible transgenic BrafV600E model, BrafV600E expression in melanocytes in utero is compatible with embryonic viability.
source: For example, BrafV600E induced in melanocytes in utero is incompatible with embryonic viability (e.g. Dankort et al., 2009), whereas in a non-inducible transgenic BrafV600E models it is not (Wurm et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wurm et al., 2012

claim: In another inducible BrafV600E model, repeated UVR exposures significantly accelerate melanoma when the oncogene is activated at 4 weeks of age.
source: We favour such an explanation rather than a mechanistic difference between the respective oncogenes (Braf vs NRAS) per se, since in another similar inducible BrafV600E model repeated UVR exposures significantly accelerate MM when the oncogene is activated at 4 weeks of age (Goel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goel et al., 2009

claim: TP53 function during the acute DNA damage response period does not contribute to protecting against transformation; it is only within the long lag phase leading to cancer development that TP53 acts as a tumour suppressor.
source: This could be somewhat akin to the work of the Evans laboratory who showed that although TP53 is very important in helping modulate the acute DNA damage response to radiation, its function in this period does not contribute to protecting against transformation, in fact it is only within the long lag phase leading to cancer development that TP53 acts as a tumour suppressor (Christophorou et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Christophorou et al., 2006

claim: Mouse models differ with respect to whether and by how much neonatal UVR accelerates melanoma.
source: Therefore, mouse models appear to differ with respect to whether and by how much neonatal UVR accelerates MM.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data comparing different models

claim: PRKDC may be an example of a modifier of melanoma in mice, but mediated by other genes of the same pathway in humans.
source: Thus PRKDC may be an example of a modifier of MM in mice, but mediated by other genes of the same pathway in humans.
evidence: Based on speculation about cross-species relevance

claim: PRKDC was one of the few DNA repair genes associated that modified melanoma risk in melanoma-prone families.
source: One can also consider Prkdc as a MM modifier gene, that is, our genetic screen detects MM modifiers in the context of a mouse model which carries a germline Cdk4 variant. In keeping with this, PRKDC was also one of the few DNA repair genes associated that modified MM risk in MM-prone families (Liang et al., 2012), many of which carry a CDKN2A mutation, and a few CDK4 mutation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2012

claim: SNPs near RRP15 are associated with human melanoma in some contexts.
source: There is some evidence that SNPs near RRP15 are also associated with human MM in some contexts. The world melanoma genetics consortium found such evidence using a method for candidate genetic association to detect variants that may not reach genome-wide statistical significance after correction for multiple testing (Schoof et al., 2012; Wurm et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schoof et al., 2012 and Wurm et al., 2012

claim: SNPs near LGAL3 and TGFB2 were the most significantly associated with melanoma risk among 39 immune-related genes tested.
source: Of the 39 immune-related genes tested, SNPs near LGAL3 and TGFB2 were the most significantly associated with MM risk (Rendleman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rendleman et al., 2013

claim: RRP15 and TGFB2 genes are located adjacent to one another and just 7 kb apart.
source: Of note, the RRP15 and TGFB2 genes are located adjacent to one another and just 7 kb apart.
evidence: Stated as genomic location information

claim: Genetic background dramatically influences the propensity for melanocyte transformation after UVR.
source: We discovered that genetic background dramatically influences the propensity for melanocyte transformation after UVR.
evidence: Based on experimental data across CC strains

claim: Depleting macrophage infiltration did not abrogate the melanoma-accelerating effect of UVR.
source: However, depleting neutrophils before and after neonatal UVR did not reduce the time of onset of MM, somewhat in line with our previous finding that depletion of macrophage infiltration also did not abrogate the MM-accelerating effect of UVR (Handoko et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Handoko et al., 2015

claim: Exome sequencing on neonatal UVR-induced mouse melanomas does not suggest a major role for UVR-induced mutagenesis.
source: But even our exome sequencing on the neonatal UVR-induced mouse melanomas does not suggest a major role for UVR-induced mutagenesis (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mukhopadhyay et al., 2016

claim: Earlier events in the few hours post UVR such as aberrant ribosome activity that can cause inappropriate protein expression may be more important than later measurable skin responses in melanoma development.
source: But our results suggest that earlier events in the few hours post UVR such as aberrant ribosome activity that can cause inappropriate protein expression, may be more important.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data

claim: In amphibians, regenerating limbs are resistant to carcinogen-induced cancer, while non-regenerating body parts are not, despite both incurring requisite DNA damage.
source: The notion of a particular constellation of gene networks that vary between CC strains and confer resistance to the MM-accelerating effects of UVR may not be dissimilar to what occurs in amphibians, where regenerating limbs, but not non-regenerating body parts, are resistant to carcinogen-induced cancer (Sarig and Tzahor, 2017), despite the fact that both anatomical sites incur the requisite DNA damage.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sarig and Tzahor, 2017

claim: Non-cancerous human skin can carry UVR signature mutations in cancer genes.
source: Hence in keeping with the fact that even non-cancerous human skin can carry UVR signature mutations in cancer genes (Martincorena et al., 2015), incorrectly repaired UVR-induced DNA damage leading to somatic mutation is in essence necessary but not sufficient to exacerbate MM, and the presence of germline variants for melanoma susceptibility and resistance is very important.
evidence: Supported by citation to Martincorena et al., 2015

claim: Incorrectly repaired UVR-induced DNA damage leading to somatic mutation is necessary but not sufficient to exacerbate melanoma.
source: Hence in keeping with the fact that even non-cancerous human skin can carry UVR signature mutations in cancer genes (Martincorena et al., 2015), incorrectly repaired UVR-induced DNA damage leading to somatic mutation is in essence necessary but not sufficient to exacerbate MM, and the presence of germline variants for melanoma susceptibility and resistance is very important.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and cited literature

claim: The presence of germline variants for melanoma susceptibility and resistance is very important for melanoma development.
source: Hence in keeping with the fact that even non-cancerous human skin can carry UVR signature mutations in cancer genes (Martincorena et al., 2015), incorrectly repaired UVR-induced DNA damage leading to somatic mutation is in essence necessary but not sufficient to exacerbate MM, and the presence of germline variants for melanoma susceptibility and resistance is very important.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and cited literature

claim: A strong quantitative trait locus for rapid onset spontaneous melanoma was mapped to Prkdc, a gene involved in detection and repair of DNA damage.
source: We mapped a strong quantitative trait locus for rapid onset spontaneous melanoma onset to Prkdc, a gene involved in detection and repair of DNA damage.

source: In contrast, rapid onset UVR-induced melanoma was linked to the ribosomal subunit gene Rrp15.

claim: Ribosome biogenesis was upregulated in skin shortly after UVR exposure.
source: Ribosome biogenesis was upregulated in skin shortly after UVR exposure.

source: Mechanistically, variation in the 'usual suspects' by which UVR may exacerbate melanoma, defective DNA repair, melanocyte proliferation, or inflammatory cell infiltration, did not explain melanoma susceptibility or resistance across the CC.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study
